correctness.reason: Direct modular matrix multiplication verifies det(X)=det(Y)=det(Z)=1, [X,Y]=[[10,5],[0,10]], [X,Y]^2=[[1,1],[0,1]], Z^3=-I, and therefore w(X,Y,Z)=-U, which is U in PSL(2,11). A single in-family witness refutes the universal omission statement.
risks: The witness says nothing by itself about full surjectivity or larger-q fibre sizes.

originality.reason: The Ore conjecture theorem of Liebeck–O'Brien–Shalev–Tiep proves every element of every finite non-abelian simple group is a commutator. For odd q>=11, a nontrivial unipotent element U of PSL(2,q) has odd prime order, so it has a square root V in its cyclic subgroup. Ore gives V=[x,y], and taking z=1 yields [x,y]^2 z^3=U. Thus a stronger published theorem already implies not merely the q=11 counterexample but failure of unipotent omission throughout the stated family.
risks: This implication uses only the standard fact that PSL(2,q) is non-abelian simple for the stated q and that squaring is bijective on an odd-order cyclic subgroup.

value.reason: The explicit q=11 triple is a concrete instantiation of the general Ore-theorem implication above. Because the universal omission claim is already mechanically impossible from a standard general theorem, the witness does not constitute a new motivated boundary result.
risks: The tuple can still serve as a regression example, but reproducibility value alone does not establish scientific value.

broader_coverage: The Ore theorem covers all elements of every finite non-abelian simple group, hence all such V in PSL(2,q).
